note: An MIT-professor pass: every line teaches the mechanism, never reads the on-screen caption. No digits, symbols or code names; every number is spoken in words.

lines: Picture the write buffer inside a storage engine. New entries land constantly, the buffer has to stay sorted, and something needs to read it while that's happening.
A balanced tree keeps its shape by rotating subtrees, and a rotation touches a handful of pointers at once, as a unit. Catch a reader mid-rotation and it sees nonsense.
So throw away the rotation entirely. Let a coin decide how tall each entry's shortcut gets, once, and never touch that decision again.
Level zero is nothing special, just the sorted list itself.
Every key also gets a tower built from coin flips: heads climbs a level, tails stops it there.
Notice what's missing from that rule — no reference to how many keys exist, or to any other key's tower.
Say half the entries that reach the first level also reach a second, because the coin is fair.
Of the entries standing on that second level, about what share climb on to a third?
answer: Each climb is its own fresh flip. A tower doesn't remember how it got to where it is, so the chance of going one level higher never changes.

lines: That forgetfulness is the entire engine behind this shape. Tilt the coin toward tails and fewer towers climb at each level; tilt it toward heads and more do.
Run the tilted coin on a real list and count: close to one climb in four survives each level under the first setting, close to one in two under the second.
Count the pointers instead of the climbs and a similar story appears: a little over one pointer per entry on average, not dozens — cheap insurance against ever rebalancing anything.
Follow one search by hand. Begin at the tallest tower on the left.
Keep moving sideways as long as the next stop is still below the target.
The instant it isn't, step down a level instead and keep going.
Every search in this structure repeats that same two-move pattern until it runs out of levels.
Imagine a list holding twenty thousand entries. Guess: does one search typically cost around twenty comparisons, around two hundred, or around two thousand?
answer: That's the logarithmic shape at work — doubling the list barely nudges the cost, which is the entire reason to climb down from a random height instead of crawling along the base.

lines: Running that exact search on twenty thousand real entries lands comfortably under thirty comparisons either way the coin is tilted, and comfortably inside the theoretical ceiling each time.
Tilt the coin further toward tails and that ceiling actually drops a little further — the original author's own argument for preferring the less even coin.
He goes further still: past a couple hundred entries, a search running triple its typical cost is, by his own estimate, a once-in-a-million event.

Here's the part that actually protects a reader. Dropping a new entry into the structure touches one pointer at each level that entry's tower reaches — nothing beyond that, no matter how large the structure already is.
Compare that to rebalancing a tree, where several pointers must flip together or the shape breaks.
One pointer at a time means a reader passing through mid-insert either sees the old picture or the new one complete — never something half-built in between.
Two pieces of software you may already rely on run exactly this idea.
A widely used storage engine's own write buffer is built this way, specifically so nothing reading it ever has to wait.

A widely used in-memory database keeps its ordered sets this way too, but tags each shortcut with how many entries it jumps over — turning 'where does this item rank' into adding up jumps instead of counting from the beginning.
Notice what was never required anywhere in this: no rebalancing step, no invariant to repair, nothing recomputed after the fact.
One random choice, made once per entry at the moment it's inserted, is the whole mechanism — and that randomness is precisely why nothing ever has to stop the readers.
One more wrinkle before we close. The same storage engine's cursor can step forward or backward through its data, yet nothing in the structure stores a backward link at all.
So how does stepping backward actually happen?
answer: By running a brand new search, aimed at finding whatever sits just below where the cursor currently is.
No backward link was ever needed. Going backward is just a forward search with a different target, costing exactly what any other search here costs.
